name: Independent on Sunday cryptic crossword No 1,868

clue.text: Bachelor travels on motorway to help girl taking train (10)

blocks.note: the standard abbreviation, as in Bachelor of Arts
someone who travels by horse, bike or bus rides
British roads are numbered this way: the M1, the M25
aid is help, and the two swap freely as noun or verb

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a journey by road, so 'taking train' invites you to add a leg by rail. It is the trailing part of a dress instead.
explanation.definitionFit: girl taking train -> BRIDESMAID: the attendant who walks behind the bride carrying the long train of her wedding dress.

clue.text: One piece of toast ample? (5)

blocks.note: a British cafe counts toast in slices, and one slice is one of these
the kindly word for a full, well-padded figure

explanation.walkthrough: Two definitions butted straight together with no joinery, which is why five words read as one breakfast order. The question mark marks the second, looser sense.
explanation.definitionFit: One piece of toast -> ROUND: a single cut slice; ample -> ROUND: of a person's body, plump and full rather than merely circular.

clue.text: Revolt suits leaders of guerrillas desperate for reform (7)

indicators.note: The leader of a word is the letter standing at its head, and the two words named after this each surrender only that one.
Something put up for reform is to be made over into a different shape, so the letters gathered up beforehand are rebuilt in another order.

blocks.note: five of the seven letters, handed over as a word before being broken up
the opening letter of each of the two words joins the pool

explanation.walkthrough: Guerrillas and revolt paint one political picture, and that is what hides the seam: the first word is the definition and the second is raw material.
explanation.definitionFit: Revolt -> DISGUST: the verb sense, as in 'it revolts me' — filling someone with nausea rather than rising up against a government.

clue.text: Aren't ropes aboard ship very good quality? (11)

indicators.note: To be aboard a vessel is to be inside it, so everything named before this ends up within the two letters that stand for the ship.

blocks.note: read as the colloquial ain't, and the apostrophe drops out as it always does in a grid
at sea a rope that has a job to do is called a line
SS is the prefix on a steamship's name, and the pair splits to sit at either end

explanation.walkthrough: 'Aren't' looks like grammar holding the question together. Read it as the slangy contraction instead and it stops being a word and becomes four letters.
explanation.definitionFit: very good quality -> SAINTLINESS: the quality of being saintly, holiness of conduct, which is goodness at its very highest pitch.

clue.text: WWI battleground Nivelle evacuated with gas coming over (7)

indicators.note: A building that is evacuated is emptied of everyone in the middle, leaving only the two standing at the doors — the first and last letters.
In a down clue what comes over something is laid on top of it, so this piece is placed above the letters that survive the emptying.

blocks.note: argon is the inert gas used in light bulbs and welding
the outer pair from the name of the French general who commanded in 1917

explanation.walkthrough: The Argonne is a forest in north-eastern France, and the Meuse-Argonne offensive of autumn 1918 was the largest battle the American army had then fought.
explanation.definitionFit: WWI battleground -> ARGONNE: the French forest where the final Allied offensive of 1918 was fought, so the name stands for the battle itself.

clue.text: Restrain mother hen (6)

blocks.note: a dam is the mother of a foal or a calf, the breeder's word that pairs with sire
a pen is a female swan, and hen serves for the female of a bird generally

explanation.walkthrough: Three words long, and the two after the definition both mean a female animal, which is what lets them read as one phrase about poultry.
explanation.definitionFit: Restrain -> DAMPEN: to dampen enthusiasm is to hold it back and take the force out of it, the figurative sense rather than wetting anything.

clue.text: Thump boyfriend admitting condition (4)

indicators.note: To admit someone is to let them in through the door, so the letters named after this go inside the pair named before.

blocks.note: BF is how a boyfriend is abbreviated in a text message
an if is the condition attached to a promise

explanation.walkthrough: Three words with nothing to skip past, which is what makes a short clue hard: 'boyfriend' looks like the subject of a sentence and is really two initials.
explanation.definitionFit: Thump -> BIFF: a biff is a smack or a blow, the comic-strip word, and it serves as noun and verb alike.

clue.text: Remote controls, absolutely loads (7)

blocks.note: but carries the sense of purely or no more than: it is but a trifle
tons of it means loads of it, the same everyday exaggeration

explanation.walkthrough: 'Remote controls' wants to be a verb phrase about operating something from a distance. It is a plural noun: the controls on a remote.
explanation.definitionFit: Remote controls -> BUTTONS: the pressable keys covering a handset, so the definition names the controls themselves rather than any act of controlling.

clue.text: Kitty met an awful arse (9)

indicators.note: Something in an awful state is in disarray, and letters in disarray have lost the order they were printed in.

blocks.note: the kitty is the pot of money a group all chips into
five letters across two little words, to be reassembled

explanation.walkthrough: FUNDAMENT is the formal, faintly medical word for the buttocks, and it shares a root with foundation: what you sit on is what you rest on.
explanation.definitionFit: arse -> FUNDAMENT: the polite anatomical word for the same part, the seat of the body, where the clue's word is the blunt one.

clue.text: Collaborator who French support when injured (8)

blocks.note: qui is the French for who, with the language named after the word it translates
the cloth loop that holds a broken arm across the chest

explanation.walkthrough: Vidkun Quisling ran Norway on Germany's behalf from 1940, and within months his surname had become the ordinary English word for anyone who does the same.
explanation.definitionFit: Collaborator -> QUISLING: someone who works with an occupying enemy against their own country, named after the Norwegian who did exactly that.

clue.text: Mother curtailed baby's insubordination (6)

indicators.note: To curtail is to dock a tail, so the word before this loses the letter at its end and keeps everything else.

blocks.note: mum is the British word for mother, and its tail comes off
a baby portion or a baby car is a tiny one

explanation.walkthrough: The surface has a parent cutting short some backchat, so the two halves of the wordplay read as one continuous sentence about a family row.
explanation.definitionFit: insubordination -> MUTINY: refusal to obey those set over you, the word reached for when a crew or a regiment turns on its officers.

clue.text: Sceptic bishop feeds tailored version of God to humanist (8,6)

indicators.note: A letter fed into something joins what is already there, so the bishop's initial goes into the pool of letters instead of standing on its own.
A tailored version has been cut and stitched into a new shape, which is what becomes of the words named after this.

blocks.note: B is the bishop on a chess scoresheet
thirteen letters, which with the bishop's one make up the full fourteen

explanation.walkthrough: 'Sceptic bishop' sounds like a churchman with private doubts, and that smooth picture is what buries the seam: only the first word is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Sceptic -> DOUBTING THOMAS: one who will not take a thing on trust, named for the apostle who insisted on seeing the wounds for himself.

clue.text: Florida city high-rise enjoys view across area (11)

indicators.note: To lie across something is to stretch right over it, so the word that follows is spanned by the pieces assembled before it.

blocks.note: a high-rise is a tall building, and it is the adjective that is wanted
A is the standard abbreviation for area
someone who enjoys good health has it
to view something is to see it

explanation.walkthrough: Not Miami and not Orlando: the state capital of Florida is a small city up in the northern panhandle, which is why the skyline in the surface misleads.
explanation.definitionFit: Florida city -> TALLAHASSEE: definition by example, since it is one city in that state — the capital, though far from the largest.

clue.text: Would it be OK if I said "cocktail"? (3,3)

indicators.note: Said means spoken out loud, so what matters about the words before it is the noise they make and not how they are spelt.

blocks.clueFragment: Would it be OK if I
blocks.note: 'Might I?' is the polite way of asking whether something would be allowed, and aloud the t slides across to open the second word

explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks are the tell: 'cocktail' is being held up as a word to be defined, and everything before it is a phrase you say out loud.
explanation.definitionFit: cocktail -> MAI TAI: the rum, lime and orgeat drink mixed in California in 1944 and poured in tiki bars ever since.

clue.text: American shot by Fritz, perhaps earlier (9)

blocks.note: A abbreviates American, and it does double duty as the nationality in the surface
Taylor Fritz is a tennis player, so a stroke of his is one example of this shot

explanation.walkthrough: 'Fritz' wants to be a German, the old wartime nickname for one. The 'perhaps' is what redirects it towards a particular named sportsman.
explanation.definitionFit: earlier -> AFOREHAND: the older form of beforehand, meaning in advance of the moment in question, and now mostly dialect.

clue.text: Nurse leant on a roll (8)

blocks.note: EN is the British qualification of enrolled nurse, the grade below a registered one
a ship that leant over to one side listed

explanation.walkthrough: 'On a roll' looks like a run of good luck, or a filling in a bap. A roll is a register of names, the muster an army keeps.
explanation.definitionFit: on a roll -> ENLISTED: to be enlisted is to have had your name written onto a regiment's roll, which is exactly being on it.

clue.text: Silence, a lack of records? (3,1,4)

blocks.note: a lack of something amounts to none of it
one recording format, the magnetic ribbon inside a cassette
the other, an extended-play disc carrying more tracks than a single

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the definition by example: two named formats stand in for records in general, and their joins fall nowhere near the answer's.
explanation.definitionFit: Silence -> NOT A PEEP: not a peep out of someone is not the faintest sound, so the phrase is an idiom for complete quiet.

clue.text: Recover gold crowns by listening (7)

indicators.note: A crown sits on top of a head, so in a down clue the piece named before this is placed above the one named after.

blocks.note: AU is gold's symbol on the periodic table, from the Latin aurum
a patient who rallies recovers strength, and so does a falling share price

explanation.walkthrough: 'Recover gold crowns' reads as dentistry or treasure, and it is that picture which disguises the middle word as loot rather than as an instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: by listening -> AURALLY: aurally means through the ear, so taking something in aurally is taking it in by listening rather than reading.

clue.text: Container of two halves, name seen in mine with lid flipped (4,3)

indicators.note: Something seen in another thing sits within it, so the letter named before this drops into the middle of the word named after.
Anything flipped is turned end over end, so the three letters it applies to are written out in the reverse order.

blocks.note: a pit is a coal mine, the word used across the British coalfields
N is the abbreviation for name on any form
the lid of a jar is its top, and this one does not stay that way up

explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a hint as well as a definition: two half-pints fill one of these, so the vessel is named by the measure it holds.
explanation.definitionFit: Container of two halves -> PINT POT: the pint mug a pub pulls beer into, holding precisely the two half-pints the definition counts out.

clue.text: Certainly, carrying knife one goes in for sharpness (6)

indicators.note: What you carry you hold within your arms, so the word before this closes right around everything that follows it.
A piece that goes in is placed inside its neighbour, splitting that word open rather than joining on at either end.

blocks.note: ay is the old spelling of aye, the word for yes certainly
to knife someone is to cut them, so the verb stands for the noun
the Roman numeral for one, a single stroke

explanation.walkthrough: The comma after the first word reads as a pause in speech, as though the setter were agreeing with you. It is there to disguise wordplay as conversation.
explanation.definitionFit: sharpness -> ACUITY: keenness of mind or of the senses — visual acuity is how sharply you see — rather than the sharpness of a blade.

clue.text: Showing equality, further education to benefit millions (7)

blocks.note: uni is the everyday British short form of university
to be for something is to be in its favour, working to its benefit
M stands for millions on a balance sheet

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is an argument about funding, and the trap is the noun everyone knows: school clothes never come into it, because the definition wants an adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Showing equality -> UNIFORM: uniform means the same all the way through, unvarying from one part to the next, which is equality across the whole.

clue.text: Ambassador among others here at four dealing with English sandwiches (14)

indicators.note: A sandwich has bread on both sides, so the two short pieces named last go one at each end of everything assembled before them.

blocks.note: re heads a memo about its subject: re your letter of the third
to be present is to be here, in the room with the rest of the company
the little word is taken exactly as it stands
four written in Roman numerals
E is the usual abbreviation on a form or a scoreboard

explanation.walkthrough: 'Ambassador among others' invites you to picture a room full of diplomats, and that smooth opening is what buries the seam after the very first word.
explanation.definitionFit: Ambassador -> REPRESENTATIVE: definition by example, an ambassador being one kind — the person sent abroad to stand and speak for a country.

clue.text: Half chance rugby doesn't start (5)

definitions.note: The answer takes a plural form but names a single set of odds — 'it's evens' — so a singular definition is fair.

indicators.note: A word that does not start has been denied the letter it would have begun with, so that first character comes off and the rest stands.

blocks.note: sevens is the seven-a-side form of the game, an Olympic sport since 2016
the letter that would have opened it is the one taken away

explanation.walkthrough: Naming a sport by the number of players a side is what lets the setter treat a whole game as a word, and the surface hides it as a scoreline.
explanation.definitionFit: Half chance -> EVENS: odds of evens mean a bet is as likely to lose as win, which is a fifty-fifty or half chance.

clue.text: One standing at the side of the room by work buffet (6)

blocks.clueFragment: One standing at the side of the room
blocks.note: the upright at the edge of a room, described at length rather than named
op is opus, a composer's numbered work

explanation.walkthrough: 'Buffet' at the end looks like a spread of food. Said the other way, to rhyme with tuffet, it means to knock about with blows.
explanation.definitionFit: buffet -> WALLOP: to buffet is to strike repeatedly, as wind buffets a roof, and to wallop is to hit hard, so both are the striking sense.

clue.text: See 6
Happy turning barge right, one managed easily (8)

indicators.note: Something turning comes round to face the other way, so the two letters before this are written out back to front.

blocks.note: someone feeling up is in high spirits, and these two letters do not stay in that order
to barge into someone is to shove them out of the way
R is right on a map or in a stage direction

explanation.walkthrough: 'Barge' is the trap: with a river of a surface around it, it reads as a boat rather than as the verb for shouldering through a crowd.
explanation.definitionFit: one managed easily -> PUSHOVER: a person or team so easily beaten that they go over at the first push, which is what makes them easy to manage.

clue.text: Neighbours' greeting, perhaps not straight across front of drive? (4)

indicators.note: To lie across something is to stretch over it from one side to the other, so the word before this closes over the single letter picked out after.
The front of a word is the letter it leads with, so only that opening character of the word after this is taken.

blocks.note: straight is the slang for heterosexual, so its opposite gives the three letters
the letter it begins with, and nothing more

explanation.walkthrough: Neighbours is the Australian soap that ran for decades on British afternoon television, so the greeting wanted is the one heard on Ramsay Street.
explanation.definitionFit: Neighbours' greeting, perhaps -> G'DAY: the Australian hello, with 'perhaps' conceding that the characters on that soap say plenty of other things too.

clue.text: Flask in bag right at the bottom (10)

indicators.note: A thing described as in another is inside it, so the word before this goes within the word after, splitting it open.

blocks.note: a net is the bag a shopper or a fisherman carries things home in
the vacuum flask that keeps tea hot, known by its brand name

explanation.walkthrough: 'Right at the bottom' reads as the last thing left in the bag, which is the joke: the words that sound like a position in the surface are the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: right at the bottom -> NETHERMOST: nethermost is the superlative of nether, meaning lowest of all, the nether regions being those below.
